html:
The Kīngitanga, or Māori King movement, began in 1858, when tribes of the central North Island chose the Waikato chief Pōtatau Te Wherowhero as their king, to unite Māori and stop land sales to settlers.

The colonial government saw it as a threat. In 1863 its troops invaded the Waikato, one of the main campaigns of the New Zealand Wars, and took much of the movement's land.

The movement survived. Te Puea Hērangi rebuilt it in the 20th century, and the Crown apologised for the Waikato invasion in 1995. The monarchy continues at Ngāruawāhia, where a new queen was crowned in 2024. See Treaty of Waitangi.
